title: Only person-to-person hantavirus sparked the cruise outbreak, but shipboard rats were not the source
dek: Andes virus is the sole hantavirus capable of person-to-person transmission; an elderly hiker brought it aboard ship from Patagonia, but the outbreak went undetected until his wife died in Johannesburg.
why: Two frontline doctors recount the detective work of investigating a rare person-to-person viral outbreak with rigorous epidemiological detail, though clinical mechanisms receive lighter treatment—ideal for those interested in field outbreak investigation.
who: Physicians, public health practitioners, and infectious disease researchers focused on field epidemiology of high-consequence pathogens and cross-border public health coordination.
skip: You can skip the opening self-introductions of both guests about their educational backgrounds and the closing chat about ‘what they would do if they weren't scientists’.

points.h: A single cruise carried thirteen hantavirus cases to thirty-three countries
points.body: The index case, an elderly hiker returned from Patagonia, boarded the cruise ship MV Hondias departing southern Argentina; he fell ill April 6 and died aboard April 11, yet the ship continued sailing. Subsequently cases appeared among passengers disembarking at different islands, including his wife, who died after going ashore in Johannesburg. In total, 13 cases were confirmed with 3 deaths, generating over 300 contacts dispersed across 33 countries and territories, triggering a massive coordinated global public health response; the WHO later declared the outbreak closed.

points.h: Only Andes virus spreads person-to-person among hantaviruses
points.body: The hantavirus family typically transmits from rodent excreta to humans via inhalation—a classic zoonotic disease with rare human-to-human spread. Andes virus is the sole exception, capable of direct person-to-person transmission. This distinction is precisely why the cruise outbreak could cascade from one infected person to many, rather than remaining an isolated spillover event.

points.h: Transmissibility begins days before symptoms appear
points.body: A 2008 Chilean prospective study following over 70 cases and 470 contacts found that infected individuals developed viremia five to fifteen days before prodromal symptoms emerged. The UK Health Security Agency adopted a pragmatic assumption that patients are infectious 48 hours before symptom onset, though definitive proof remains absent; empirical evidence does support transmission during the prodromal phase. This means waiting until someone ‘looks sick’before isolating may already be too late.

points.h: Outbreak came from a person, not rats aboard ship
points.body: Some questioned whether rats stowed aboard the ship triggered the outbreak—rodents can indeed climb mooring cables. However, cables were fitted with rodent guards, the vessel held valid rodent certification, and quarantine inspections at South Georgia deployed detection dogs without finding rodents. Environmental swabs of cabin dust yielded no rodent genomic material, only viral RNA detected in infected passengers' quarters and not in other cabins. The near-identical genetic sequences across 12 cases (maximum 1 SNP difference) further supported person-to-person spread rather than a separate rodent source aboard.

points.h: Long incubation masked the outbreak's detection for weeks
points.body: Cruise ship deaths are not exceptional, particularly among aging passengers, so the index case's death was not initially flagged as alarming. Only after his wife fell ill approximately 18 days post-disembarkation and ultimately died in Johannesburg, and after a physician on Ascension Island connected these scattered cases, was the outbreak signal formally reported in early May, prompting swift WHO action.

points.h: One doctor evacuated twenty-five exposed contacts alone across the ocean
points.body: Catherine flew to Tenerife alone to escort 25 exposed contacts for evacuation. Standard protocol for doffing high-level PPE requires a second person present for oversight; she improvised by training a crew member aboard the aircraft as her backup. With passengers in the high-risk incubation window, she sketched a seating diagram before departure designating a quarantine zone—if anyone fell ill mid-flight, the rear rows would isolate them, and passengers and crew would use separate lavatories. The 48-hour flight concluded with no passenger illness.

points.h: Immune dysregulation, not viral destruction, drives fatal cardiopulmonary syndrome
points.body: Chilean researcher Pablo Vial argues that Andes virus is not cytolytic; cardiopulmonary syndrome emerges from epithelial membrane dysfunction—a functional derangement, not direct viral cytotoxicity. The real danger lies in late-stage immune response, not the virus itself: the body initially tolerates infection until tolerance collapses. This also explains why late-course antivirals show no clear benefit in reducing viral load.

points.h: Monoclonal antibodies existed but couldn't be tested in humans
points.body: Monoclonal antibodies targeting Andes virus exist and demonstrated efficacy in hamster models, but because they had not undergone human safety evaluation, they were not deployed in this outbreak, even as investigational therapy. The UK instead provided favipiravir for post-exposure prophylaxis to 19 high-risk contacts; however, since these individuals might never have been infected, attributing any protection to the drug remains difficult. Whether to prefer monoclonal antibodies or antivirals for post-exposure prevention remains an open research question.
